I would argue for a First Contract exception. If you draft a player or trade for them while on their rookie deal their contract is discounted against the cap 1% for every year of service. Example: a player signs a max contract with 10 years of service for 35% of the cap. That contract only counts as 25% of the cap. If a team goes into the second apron while they are using the FCE they lose the ability to use that exception for 3 years. You only have one FCE exception to use every year. The idea is you give teams extra flexibility to build around their stars as they age. Everyone wants stars to stay with the team drafted them and I think most people don’t want to watch aging superstars waste their post prime on terrible teams. 10% isn’t going push a team from average to contender but it might give enough flexibility for a team to go from good to contender.

The point I would like to highlight is how much health impacts the surplus value of a player. You want to be careful not to over-index on ex-post injury data when evaluating ex-ante contract decisions. I.E., a player's contract at signing should account for injury risk. If a player does not get injured, their contract *should* look team friendly. The max or near max contracts where a player gets to 0 VOSE without a major injury are *terrible* contracts. In the best case scenario you're a play-in team, and with injuries (and you should expect someone to miss time with injury at some point) you're deep in the lottery. Keep that in mind when estimating a 'fair' contract for a player coming off a fully healthy season.

Every team, every season, sees roughly 4-5% more of their shots get assisted when Luka is off the court than when he's one it. This is not saying that he's a bad offensive player or that he makes the offense less efficient or anything....but there's clearly less passing when he's on the court.

The top comment is right about the percentage, but the number that actually measures spacing isn't percentage at all. It's attempts. A guy shooting 35% on real volume gets guarded past the line, because his defender has to respect it. A guy at 40% who takes two a game does not, because his defender has already done that math. Spacing is entirely about whether the defender leaves, and only volume makes him leave. So for this roster I'd look at 3PA per 36 across the starters rather than their percentages. That'll tell you how much room the drives actually have.

Worth being careful with EPM over 22 games specifically. It's a predictive metric with a box-score prior sitting underneath the plus-minus side, and at playoff-sized samples the prior is doing a lot of the work. So a +10.5 over 14 games reads closer to "the model already expected him to be roughly this good and the on-off didn't argue with it" than to a clean measurement of what happened in those games. That isn't a knock on Wemby or on EPM. It's that being the most reliable full-season metric and being a measurement of one playoff run are two different claims, and the LeBron 2009 comparison quietly assumes they're the same one.

The sample size objection is the one everyone reaches for first, but I think the bigger problem is that there's no baseline here. Cup finalists are by construction teams that were already good enough to win a group and then three straight elimination games. To know whether making the final tells you anything extra, you need to know how often a team of that quality reaches the conference finals anyway. If that answer turns out to be roughly four in six, the cup told you nothing their record hadn't already. The comparison that would actually settle it is cup finalists against non-finalists with similar net ratings the same season. Six data points is thin for that, but it's the right shape of question, and the current version can't separate "the cup is predictive" from "good teams win things."

The top-4 selection is doing a lot of work here, and I think you can get the same answer without needing it. If expansion dilutes talent, the thing that should move is the spread of the league rather than any particular team's win total. So the standard deviation of net rating across all teams is a cleaner measurement, and it doesn't require assuming in advance who the beneficiaries are. Win totals also quietly confound two different things: how good a team was, and how much weaker its schedule got. Net rating spread separates those. If the sd jumps in expansion years and settles afterwards, that's exactly the effect you're describing, measured without picking a subgroup first.

I’ve always thought one way to look at this is through the distribution of wins or net ratings across the league. In a top-heavy season, you get a flatter, more spread-out bell curve, while in a league where teams are more evenly matched, you get a tighter distribution. An all-time team can make a single season look unusually uneven, but if you look across multiple years, you can start to see a broader trend showing that, in certain periods, it was simply easier for the best teams to pile up wins. If you look at the variance in net rating by decade: 80s: 19 90s: 29 00s: 22.5 10s: 23 These eras also had roughly similar league-average ORTGs, with the 2000s and 2010s being slightly lower. Expansion made the entire league more top-heavy and gave a lot of teams extra wins. Even compared to the 2010s, which had plenty of top-heavy seasons, nothing really matches the expansion-era 90s. That spread peaked from 1995 to 1998, when the NBA had expanded to 29 teams and the Bulls were at the peak of their powers.
